Iceland
EYES-land
n. (the North Atlantic island whose Reformation gave it a complete Bible in its own tongue in 1584, and whose last Catholic bishop was beheaded)
Icelandic Ísland, the land of ice, named by the Norse settlers of the ninth century; the tongue is the most conservative of the Scandinavian languages.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Iceland is the remote island where the Reformation arrived by royal decree and produced, almost at once, one of the best vernacular Bibles in Europe. Danish officials brought the ordinance of 1537 and met resistance; Jon Arason, bishop of Holar and the last Catholic bishop in Iceland, held the north against it, raised men, and was taken and beheaded with his two sons at Skalholt in November 1550 without trial, an act the dictionary names as judicial murder whatever his doctrine. What the Reformation did well in Iceland was translate. Oddur Gottskalksson, a bishop's son who had learned Lutheran doctrine abroad, translated the New Testament into Icelandic in a cowshed at Skalholt, as the story goes, and it was printed at Roskilde in 1540, the first book ever printed in Icelandic. Gudbrandur Thorlaksson, bishop of Holar for over fifty years from 1571, set up a press at Holar, revised and completed the whole Bible, and printed it there in 1584 in five hundred copies, enough for every church in the country, a book so good that its language is still a standard. The dictionary enters Iceland because a population of perhaps fifty thousand on a volcanic island got a whole printed Bible in their own speech before most of Europe did.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a press as a machine for printing; a cowshed as a shelter for cattle; beheading as the act of severing the head; and an edition as the whole number of copies published at once.

expand to see more

PRESS, n. A machine for printing; the art or business of printing and publishing.

SHED, n. A slight or temporary building; a penthouse or hovel; a covering for shelter.

BEHEAD, v. To cut off the head; to sever the head from the body with a cutting instrument.

EDITION, n. The publication of any book; the whole number of copies of a work published at once.

ISLAND, n. A tract of land surrounded with water; a piece of land not connected with a continent.

Key Scripture

Isa 42:4 — "He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law."

Psa 97:1 — "The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof."

Isa 51:5 — "My righteousness is near; my salvation is gone forth, and mine arms shall judge the people; the isles shall wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust."

Isa 49:1 — "Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far; The LORD hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name."

Modern Corruption

North Atlantic island reformed by royal ordinance in 1537, whose last Catholic bishop was beheaded in 1550 and whose complete Icelandic Bible was printed at Holar in 1584.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the execution without trial of a defeated opponent, which is what happened to Jon Arason and his sons at Skalholt in 1550. He had taken up arms against the royal officers, and the dictionary neither approves his doctrine nor his rising; it holds that a man captured in such a quarrel is owed a hearing and a sentence, and that the Danish officials who had him beheaded on their own authority committed murder. The rule of the kingdom is not changed by the convenience of the executioner, and the isles that wait for the Lord's law “shall wait for his law” (Isa 42:4) also wait for his justice.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the promise made to the islands and the far places, which Iceland fulfils as exactly as any country in Europe. “Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far” (Isa 49:1) is addressed to men at the edge of the known world, and the response is the psalm's, “let the multitude of isles be glad thereof” (Psa 97:1). Five hundred Bibles printed at Holar in 1584, one for every church on the island, is what “the isles shall wait upon me” (Isa 51:5) came to mean in Icelandic.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew iy (H339), an island, a coastland; Hebrew torah (H8451), law, instruction; Hebrew yachal (H3176), to wait, to hope.

expand to see more

Hebrew iy (H339) — an island, a coast, a maritime land; “the isles shall wait for his law”, Isaiah 42:4.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, direction; “and the isles shall wait for his law”, Isaiah 42:4.

Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, to hearken; “Listen, O isles, unto me”, Isaiah 49:1.

Hebrew samach (H8055) — to rejoice, to be glad; “let the multitude of isles be glad thereof”, Psalm 97:1.

Hebrew yachal (H3176) — to wait, to hope, to tarry for; “the isles shall wait upon me”, Isaiah 51:5.

Usage

"“Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far” (Isa 49:1) — the Icelandic New Testament printed in 1540."

"“let the multitude of isles be glad thereof” (Psa 97:1) — five hundred whole Bibles printed at Holar in 1584."

"“the isles shall wait for his law” (Isa 42:4) — a bishop beheaded without trial at Skalholt in 1550."
